blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define fiscal policy, name its three working parts, and tell it apart from its monetary neighbour.

blocks.heading: Fiscal policy, defined
blocks.text: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy. It works through the budget: each year the government sets out what it will spend, what it will raise in taxes, and what it will borrow where the two do not match - and each of those three decisions moves the economy. The word itself comes from the state's purse: fiscal questions are budget questions, and a change to any of the three levers counts as a fiscal measure.

blocks.heading: The budget as instrument
blocks.text: The yearly budget is the instrument of the stance: in the Netherlands, budget day each September sets the year's tax and spending plans together, and it is through those plans - not through any single decree - that the fiscal stance changes. A Namibian illustration: a year in which the budget raises the gravel-road programme and lifts the tax-free allowance is a year of changed fiscal policy, whatever else stays the same, and a year in which the two levers are held is a year the stance is unchanged.

blocks.heading: Fiscal against monetary
blocks.text: Fiscal policy is budget policy: spending, taxation and borrowing, decided by the government in the budget. Its counterpart works through the price of borrowing money and the lending of banks - monetary policy, which belongs to topic 4.4 and is named here only to mark the boundary. A finance minister changing a tax rate is acting fiscally; a central bank changing the cost of credit is not, whatever the newspapers call it. Keeping the two apart is a real boundary, and the test is which authority sets the measure: the budget's levers are fiscal, the lenders' price is not.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The aims both policies serve are set out in topic 4.2; the interest-rate route to them is topic 4.4.
